children.html: The benefits of being self-compassionate on days when interactions with body-focused others are frequent
Allison C. Kelly∗, Kathryn E. Miller, Elizabeth Stephen
Department of Psychology, University of Waterloo, Waterloo, ON, Canada
a r t i c l e i n f o
Article history: Received 8 June 2016 Received in revised form 12 October 2016 Accepted 12 October 2016 Available online 29 October 2016
Keywords: Self-compassion Body image Body appreciation Intuitive eating Social interactions Within persons
a b s t r a c t

We examined whether a woman's level of self-compassion on a given day (within-persons) and over a week (between-persons)influenced her eating, body image, and affectin the face of frequent daily and/or weekly interactions with body-focused others. For seven nights, 92 female undergraduates reported on their daily social interactions, self-compassion, body image, eating, and affect. On days when women were less self-compassionate than usual, frequent interactions with body-focused others were associated with more body image concerns and negative affect, and less body appreciation and intuitive eating. However, these relationships were absent or inversed on days when women were more self-compassionate than usual. Self-compassion played a similar buffering role at the between-persons level. Results suggest that by treating themselves with a higher degree of self-compassion than what is typical for them, young women may be able to maintain healthier approaches to eating and body image when faced with body image threats.

There is a wealth of evidence indicating that exposure to individuals who are preoccupied with dieting and body image concerns is costly for one's own body image and eating habits. Gravener, Haedt, Heatherton, and Keel (2008) found that young adult women who perceived their peers to be dieting were more concerned with becoming thin themselves. In addition, studies have found that women whose friends engage in dieting behaviors are at elevated risk of current and future eating disorder symptoms (Eisenberg & Neumark-Sztainer, 2010; Hutchinson, Rapee, & Taylor, 2010; Keel, Forney, Brown, & Heatherton, 2013; Peterson, Paulson, & Williams, 2007; Shomaker & Furman, 2009). There is also a large research literature showing that simply hearing a peer make self-disparaging comments about her body or eating habits, also known as "fat talk," increases body dissatisfaction in the listener (Clarke, Murnen, & Smolak, 2010; Stice, Maxfield, & Wells, 2003). The negative eating and body image consequences of interactions with body-focused others reveal the importance of identifying the factors that might protect women in the face of these social threats, and help them maintain a healthy approach to eating and body image.

Self-compassion has recently emerged as an important protective factor against threats to body image (see Braun, Park, and Gorin (2016) for a review) and as a facilitator of positive forms of body image (e.g., Andrew, Tiggemann, & Clark, 2016; Schoenefeld & Webb, 2013). At its essence, self-compassion is compassion that is directed inward and can therefore be defined as an awareness of and sensitivity toward personal suffering coupled with a commitment to prevent and alleviate this suffering (Dalai Lama, 1995; Gilbert, 2009). Most empirical research on this construct relies on Neff's (2003) operational definition of self-compassion as comprised of self-kindness, mindfulness, and common humanity. These respectively entail responding to personal distress and disappointment with care and understanding rather than judgment, balanced rather than magnified attention, and the belief that suffering unites rather than divides human beings. Just like self-esteem, self-compassion is a positive self-attitude, and the two variables are moderately correlated (Neff, 2003). However, self-esteem derives from an assessment of one's qualities and attributes, and can thus fluctuate with achievements and setbacks; conversely, self-compassion is a care-based form of positive regard that promotes self-acceptance even in the face of failure (Leary, Tate, Adams, Batts Allen, & Hancock, 2007). Empirical studies have found that self-compassion accounts for unique variance in mental health outcomes beyond self-esteem, and in the domain of body image and eating behaviors, often explains even more variance
(Kelly, Vimalakanthan, & Carter, 2014; Wasylkiw, MacKinnon, & MacLellan, 2012).

Because self-compassion is a response to feeling upset or inadequate, its benefits in the body image realm should be especially evident when individuals are exposed to known triggers or correlates of body dissatisfaction. Several studies have found support for this notion. Kelly, Vimalakanthan, and Miller (2014) found that college women who had a higher body mass index (BMI), which is generally associated with more eating pathology and body dissatisfaction, did indeed endorse these features but only if they had low or moderate levels of self-compassion.Among women who had high levels of self-compassion, BMI was unrelated to eating pathology and body image. Tylka, Russell, and Neal(2015) similarly found that perceived sociocultural pressures to be thin were associated withahigher level ofinternalizationofthe thinideal among women with low and average, but not high, levels of self-compassion. Other studies have similarly found that the links between various threats to body image – including the tendencies to make body comparisons, survey one's body from an observer's perspective, and base one's self-worth on appearance – were more strongly related to negative body image in women who were lower in self-compassion (Homan & Tylka, 2015; Liss & Erchull, 2015). Together, these studies offer empirical support for the notion that a higher level of self-compassion may protect women from the potentially negative consequences and correlates of body image threats.

Self-compassion is typically conceptualized as a trait (Neff, 2003), and most research on the topic, including in the body image domain, has investigated its relationship to other variables at the between-persons level. That is, studies have investigated differences between people (usually women) in their overall levels of self-compassion to understand differences in the way these people eat and feel about their bodies. As with other personality variables (Fleeson, 2001; Moskowitz, Brown, & Côté, 1997), however, selfcompassion levels vary not only between persons but also within a person. Indeed, daily diary studies reveal that between 37 and 42% of the variance in undergraduate students' self-compassion levels occur within-persons (Breines, Toole, & Chen, 2014; Kelly & Stephen, 2016; Zuroff, Kelly, Leybman, & Gilbert, 2012), indicating that there are substantial fluctuations in a given person's level of self-compassion from one day to the next. Experimental studies also reveal that it is possible to increase self-compassion levels both momentarily and over time (Albertson, Neff, & Dill-Shackleford, 2015; Kelly, Wisniewski, Matin-Wagar, & Hoffman (in press); Leary et al., 2007), further supporting the idea that levels of self-compassion can vary within a person. Therefore, it appears that in addition to examining the role thatindividuals'typical or average level of self-compassion plays with regards to their body image and eating, it may also be worthwhile to examine whether fluctuations in their own personal levels of self-compassion are important.

To address this question, Breines et al. (2014) conducted a fourday study in which college women reported on their daily level of appearance-related self-compassion. The authors found that participants had less disordered eating on days when they had a higher level of self-compassion than usual vis-à-vis their appearance concerns (i.e., a level of self-compassion that was higher than their personal mean level over the four days). In a seven-day daily diary study, Kelly and Stephen (2016) also found that on days when college women treated themselves more self-compassionately than usual, they reported eating in a more intuitive (i.e., eating based on hunger and satiety) and less restrictive way, and also reported a higher level of body appreciation and body satisfaction. Together, these two studies suggest that among college women, variability in
levels of self-compassion from one day to the next are associated with variability in body image and eating experiences.

Given that self-compassion is a way of responding to stress and distress, an important next step is to examine whether within a given person, fluctuations in levels of self-compassion influence the way she copes when faced with body image stressors in daily life. In other words, it will be important to build on the aforementioned studies of within-persons relationships, which examined the main effects of self-compassion, by investigating whether self-compassion interacts with body image stressors atthe within-persons level to predict eating and body image. Although a fairly large body of literature now shows that women who have a higher level of self-compassion than others (i.e., between-persons level of self-compassion) are more protected from body image threat(s) (Homan & Tylka, 2015; Tylka et al., 2015), these studies have been cross-sectional and only allow us to conclude that being a person who is generally high in self-compassion offers protection from generally high levels of body image threats. It therefore remains unknown whether within a given individual, a self-compassionate response during periods of high body image stress offers benefits during these stressful times. Addressing this gap would not only provide a stronger test of current theorizing on self-compassion, but would also provide evidence to support the idea that independent of one's typical level of self-compassion, cultivating self-compassion during periods of body image stress can help to preserve more adaptive forms of body image and eating during these periods.

Our first and primary objective was to examine the withinpersons interaction between self-compassion and frequency of interactions with body-focused others in predicting criteria variables. To explore this research question, multiple repeated measurements from a given person over time are required. We therefore asked participants to provide nightly ratings, for seven days, of how self-compassionate they were and how frequently they interacted with body-focused others each day. We operationalized within-persons self-compassion as the extent to which a participant's level of self-compassion on a given day deviated from her personal mean level of self-compassion across study days. Within-persons social interactions with body-focused others similarly represented the difference between a participant's frequency of interactions with body-focused others on a given day and that participant's personal mean frequency of interactions across study days. The statistical interaction between these two within-persons variables would allow us to examine our research questions.

Given the growing emphasis on distinguishing between adaptive and maladaptive functioning in the body image domain, we examined intuitive eating (i.e., eating in accordance with hunger and satiety signals rather than dietary rules) and body appreciation (i.e., acceptance of and respect for one's body) as indicators of the former, and body image concerns and negative affect as indicators of the latter. We chose this subset of variables because of the research showing that various forms exposure to body-focused others can influence eating, body appreciation, body image concerns, and negative affect (Jones, Crowther, & Ciesla 2014; Paxton, Schutz, Wertheim, & Muir, 1999; Wasylkiw & Butler, 2014).

We hypothesized that more interactions with body-focused others on a given day would be associated with a lower level of intuitive eating and body appreciation, and a higher level of body image concerns and negative affect, but only on days when women were less self-compassionate than usual. On days when women were more self-compassionate than usual, we expected that these relationships would be absent or inversed. We reasoned that relationships might be inversed because self-compassion is a form of

self-relating that occurs at times of stress and distress specifically (Gilbert, 2005; Neff, 2003); therefore, its benefits should be most salient on days when interactions with body-focused others are frequent.

Our second objective was to examine the between-persons interaction between self-compassion and frequency of interactions with body-focused others. Specifically, we sought to examine whether women's mean level of self-compassion over the week would moderate the relationship between their mean frequency of interactions with body-focused others over the week and their mean levels of intuitive eating, body appreciation, body image concerns, and negative affect. By aggregating participants' self-reports across the multiple study days, this research would extend previous cross-sectional research showing that self-compassion buffers the relationship between body image threats and outcomes at the between-persons level. We hypothesized that young adult women who had more frequentinteractions with body-focused others over the week would report lower average levels of intuitive eating and body appreciation and higher average levels of body image concerns and negative affect if they had lower but not higher mean levels of self-compassion relative to their peers.

As described in Kelly and Stephen (2016), participation in this study was available to all female undergraduate students enrolled in the university psychology subject pool, and was described as a study investigating personality, feelings, and body image. For seven consecutive days, participants were asked to complete a nightly survey e-mailed to them via a link to an online survey. Instructions were to complete these nightly surveys anytime between 4 and 11pm each day; this time frame ensured that participants with varying class schedules would be able to report on their day's experiences. Credit was awarded for every survey completed on time. In addition, participants were allowed to miss one survey and complete a make-up survey on Day 8.

One-hundred and forty-three college women consented to participate in the study. Ofthese, 32 completed three or fewer surveys, and so were removed because we feltthey provided too few assessment points to allow for an adequate examination of within-person fluctuations. An additional 15 participants were removed because they failed to complete their surveys during the required time frames, and another four were removed because they had outlying BMIs (over 40). Our final sample consisted of 92 females. The mean number of daily surveys completed across these participants was 6.67 (SD = 1.2), with 83% of them completing six or more surveys.

Mean age in the sample was 19.7 (SD = 1.93) and the ethnic breakdown was: 50% Caucasian, 21% East Asian, 1.6% Southeast Asian, 4.8% Black/African, 9.7% South Asian, 1.6% Middle Eastern, 1.6% West Indian/Caribbean, 1.6% Aboriginal, and 8.1% unknown. BMI, calculated based on self-reported weight and height (kg/m2), ranged from 15.6 to 35 in the sample, with a mean of 22.62 (SD = 3.41). A histogram together with kurtosis and skewness values (1.45 and 0.96 respectively) revealed that the BMI distribution in our sample approximated a normal curve.
In all measures, instructions were modified to orient participants to their present day's experiences, and items were thus reworded from the present tense to the past tense.

Interactions with body-focused others. Participants were asked to rate the frequency of interactions they had with bodyfocused others each day. Because there was no existing, validated measure designed to assess this construct at a state or daily level, we developed a face valid measure brief enough to be included in a battery of daily diary measures. The measure asked participants to respond to a 5-item question using a scale from 1 (not at all) to 5 (constantly). "Today, how often did you interact with people who. . ." (a) "were talking about dieting?"; (b) "were focused on body image?"; (c) "were focused on exercise and working out?"; (d) "had 'normal' eating habits (i.e., people who eat flexibly without being restrictive or overly preoccupied with calories)"; and (e) "focus little on body image." The first three items were designed to measure frequency of interactions with body-focused others and the latter two were designed to assess frequency of interactions with non-body-focused others, which was not of interest in the present paper.

We conducted a principal components analysis (PCA) on all five items, and this yielded a scree plot suggestive of two factors. A promax rotation resulted in two uncorrelated factors (r = .08). Given this orthogonality, we applied a varimax rotationand found thatthe two factors explained 23.5% and 17.1% of the variance. As expected, the firstthree items loaded onto the firstfactor (dietfocus .87, body focus .94, exercise focus .83), and the lasttwo onto the second factor (flexible eating .91, little body focus .91). No item cross-loaded onto the other factor at more than .20. Of interest to the present paper was the firstfactor, which we called "frequency of interactions with body-focused others." This factor's internal consistency was high, with Cronbach's alphas ranging from .85 to .89 across study days.

Self-compassion. Participants completed a modified version of the Self-Compassion Scale-Short Form (SCS-SF; Raes, Pommier, Neff, & Van Gucht, 2011), which asked them to report on the extent to which they responded to personal distress and setbacks on that particular day with self-compassion (e.g., "I tried to be understanding andpatienttowards those aspects ofmypersonality Idon'tlike," "Itried to see my failings as part ofthe human condition."). The SCS-SF has 12 items, rated from 1 (almost never) to 5 (almost always). In their three-sample validation study, Raes et al. found that the total SCS-SF score correlated near perfectly (r ≥ .97) with Neff's (2003) full 26-item Self-Compassion and had Cronbach's alphas of .86 or more, demonstrating adequate internal consistency. The Cronbach's alpha for the total score in our sample ranged from .87 to .91 across study days.

Intuitive eating. Intuitive eating was assessed withthe 23-item Intuitive Eating Scale-2 (IES-2; Tylka & Kroon Van Diest, 2013). This measure assesses the extent to which individuals eat based on hunger, cravings, and satiety, rather than dietary rules using a scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). In the present study, participants responded to items based on their present day's experiences. Sample items included: "If I was craving a certain food, I allowed myself to have it" and "I trusted my body to tell me how much to eat." Scores on the IES-2 have demonstrated good reliability, internal consistency, and validity (Tylka & Kroon Van Diest, 2013). In the present study, Cronbach's alphas ranged from .87 to .90 across days.
Body appreciation. Body appreciation, which refers to feeling and displaying respect and gratitude toward one's body, was

measured with the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS; Avalos, Tylka, & Wood-Barcalow, 2005). The BAS consists of 13 items rated from 1 (never) to 5 (always). Items included "I felt that my body had at least some good qualities" and "I engaged in healthy behaviors to take care of my body," which participants rated based on their experiences on that particular day. Avalos et al. found that scores on the BAS have good internal-consistency, test-retest reliability, and construct validity. In the present study, internal consistency was strong with Cronbach's alphas ranging from .95 to .96 across study days.

Body image concerns. Body image concerns were assessed with three items derived from the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q; Fairburn & Beglin, 1994): "I have had a definite fear that I might gain weight," "My weight has influenced how I think about (judge) myself as a person," and "My shape has influenced how I think about (judge) myself as a person." Participants rated these items from 1 (not at all) to 5 (frequently) based on that day's experiences. This 5-point rating scale was used instead of the 0-6 rating scale from the EDE-Q in order to be consistent with all other daily measures in the study. Mean scores on this measure of body image concerns correlated strongly with participants' scores on the Weight Concerns (r = .77, p < .001) and Shape Concerns (r=.73, p<.001) subscales of the EDE-Q, completed roughly a week before the daily diary portion of the study began, supporting the measure's convergent validity as an indicator of body image concerns. Cronbach's alphas for this measure ranged from .90 to .92 across study days.

Negative affect. Negative affect was assessed with the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS; Watson, Clark, & Tellegen, 1988), which consists of 20 items that assess both positively and negatively-valenced forms of affect. For the purpose of the present analyses, only the 10 negative affect items were examined. These included "afraid," "distressed," "irritable," and "guilty," which participants rated from 1 (very slightly or not at all) to 5 (extremely) based on how they felt on that particular day. Scores on the PANAS have demonstrated strong convergent and discriminant validity (Watson et al., 1988). In the present study, Cronbach's alphas for negative affect ranged from .91 to .93 across study days.

Multilevel modeling is the ideal data analytic approach when examining hierarchical data structures, such as those from daily diary studies in which assessment days are nested within participants. It takes into account the variance that is shared across the various self-reported data provided by a given participant and disaggregates this between-persons level-2 variance from the within-persons level-1 variance—that is, the variance accounted for by the particular assessment day. Multilevel modeling with maximum likelihood estimation uses all of the available within and between-person data to estimate parameters, thus overcoming the problem of biased samples or of biased imputation techniques (Snijders & Bosker, 2012). As such, the approach makes it possible to retain all available data from participants for whom observations are missing, an inevitable occurrence in studies that administer multiple repeated measures over time (see Snijders & Bosker, 1999).

Before multilevel models were run, all predictor variables were disaggregated into within- and between-persons variance. For a given predictor, a between-persons variable was created for each participant using the mean of her scores across study days. Withinpersons variables were then computed by subtracting participants' raw score on a given day from their mean score across study days. These within-person variables therefore represented a partic-

ipant's daily deviation from her personal mean weekly score. Before conducting analyses, both between- and within-persons predictor variables were centered around a mean of 0. We chose not to standardize the standard deviations of predictor variables given that each participant in the daily diary study has her own unique standard deviation, and the standardizing procedure would eliminate these meaningful differences. Therefore, in multilevel models, a coefficient of 1 for a given predictor would indicate that as scores on that measure went up by 1 unit, so too did scores on the criteria variable measure. Of note, all measures in the study used a 5-point scale making this metric easy to interpret across models.

Four multilevel models were run in SAS 9.3 with raw scores on intuitive eating, body appreciation, body image concerns, and negative affect across study days serving as the criteria variables. BMI was entered as a covariate fixed effect in all models given the possibility of it relating to criteria variables. Model 1 additionally contained the within-persons and between-persons fixed effects for frequency of interactions with body-focused others, i.e., daily frequency and weekly frequency. It also contained the withinand between-persons fixed effects for self-compassion, i.e., daily self-compassion and weekly self-compassion. In Model 2, which was of greatest relevance to our hypotheses, interaction terms between self-compassion and frequency of interactions with bodyfocused others were added at each level of analysis—namely, Daily Self-Compassion × Daily Frequency at the within-persons level and Weekly Self-Compassion × Weekly Frequency at the betweenpersons level. Significant interactions were probed with simple slope estimates to determine the relationship between frequency of interactions with body-focused others and the given criterion variable when self-compassion levels were low (1 scale unit below the mean), average (the mean), and high (1 scale unit above the mean). Means and standard deviations were computed for participants' mean scores on daily diary variables across study days, and are presented in Table 1. Intraclass correlations (ICCs) were also computed for all daily diary variables. ICCs represent the proportion of total variance in a variable that occurs at the between-persons level. As presented in Table 1, interactions with body-focused others and negative affect had the lowest ICCs, with approximately half of the variance in these variables occurring at the between-persons level. These values indicate that interactions with body-focused others and levels of negative affect differed roughly as much between participants over the week as they did within participants from one day to the next. Between-persons variance accounted for approximately two-thirds of the variance in self-compassion and intuitive eating and over three-quarters of the variance in body appreciation and body image concerns. Daily self-compassion was unrelated to daily levels of body image concerns and frequency of interactions with body-focused others. Daily frequency of interactions with body-focused others was associated with more daily body image concerns at a trend level, but was unrelated to all other variables. At the between-persons level, BMI was negatively associated with body appreciation and positively associated with body image concerns. Furthermore, a higher mean level of self-compassion over the week was associated with a higher mean level of intuitive eating and body appreciation, as previously reported by Kelly and Stephen (2016), and with lower mean levels of body image concerns and negative affect. Frequency of interactions with body-focused others was unrelated to self-compassion at the between-persons level, but was related to criteria variables. Specifically, more frequent interactions with body-focused others over the week was related to lower mean levels of intuitive eating and body appreciation (p = .061) and higher mean levels of body image concerns and negative affect.

Table 2 presents results from our central analyses, with main effects presented under "Model 1" in each table. Because these main effects were not the focus of the current paper, and some have previously been reported by Kelly and Stephen (2016), the text below only reports on the interactions that address the present research questions.

Intuitive eating. As seen in Table 2, there was a significant within-persons interaction between self-compassion and frequency of interactions with body-focused others in predicting intuitive eating. Consistent with our predictions, simple slope estimates showed that a higher daily frequency of interactions with body-focused others was associated with less intuitive eating (p = .036) on days when participants were less self-compassionate than usual, but this relationship was inversed on days when participants were more self-compassionate than usual (p = .003) (see Table 3). There was also a significant between-persons interaction between self-compassion and frequency of interactions with bodyfocused others. As seen in Table 4, a higher mean frequency of interactions with body-focused others over the week was associated with a lower mean level of intuitive eating among participants who had lower (p=.001) and average (p=.002) mean levels of self-compassion, but was unrelated to intuitive eating among participants who had higher mean levels of self-compassion.

Simple slope estimates revealed that a higher mean frequency of interactions with body-focused others across study days was associated with a lower mean level of body appreciation among participants with low (p = .001) or average (p = .018) levels of self-compassion over the week, but was unrelated to body appreciation among participants who had high mean levels of selfcompassion over the week (see Table 4).

Body image concerns. Consistent with our hypotheses, there was a within-persons interaction between self-compassion and frequency of interactions with body-focused others in predicting body image concerns at a trend-level (p = .092; see Table 2). Simple slope estimates, presented in Table 3, revealed that daily frequency of interactions with body-focused others was positively related to body image concerns on days when individuals were less self-compassionate thanusual(p = .006) and ondays whenthey displayed their typical level of self-compassion (p = .001); however, this relationship was absent on days when participants were more self-compassionate than usual. There was no between-persons interaction between self-compassion and frequency of interactions with body-focused others in predicting body image concerns, p = .144.
Negative affect. There was a significant within-persons interaction between self-compassion and frequency of interactions with body-focused others in predicting negative affect (see Table 2). As

seen in Table 3, frequency of interactions with body-focused others was positively related to negative affect (p = .026) on days when participants were less self-compassionate than usual but negatively related to negative affect(p = .048) on days when participants were more self-compassionate than usual. At the between-persons level, self-compassion and frequency of interactions with bodyfocused others did not interact to predict negative affect, p = .926 (see Table 2).

Post-hoc analyses. Our measure assessing frequency of interactions with body-focused others consisted of three items that loaded onto one internally consistent factor. It is nevertheless possible that the individual items may have related differently to criteria variables and/or have interacted in different ways with selfcompassion to predict outcomes. As a result, we first conducted zero-order correlations between each item – namely, interactions with diet-focused others, interactions with body-focused others, and interactions with exercise-focused others – and each of our criteria variables at the within- and between-persons level. Binary relationships demonstrated the same pattern with the individual items as they did with the composite measure, with significant correlations remaining significant and similar in magnitude, and nonsignificant correlations remaining nonsignificant. We additionally re-ran all the multilevel analyses listed above substituting the composite frequency variable with each of its three items. At the within-persons level, these items generally interacted with daily self-compassion in the same way as the composite. The only exceptions were that there was no interaction between daily self-compassion and frequency of interactions with body-focused others in predicting negative affect, or between daily self-compassion and interactions with exercise-focused others in predicting body appreciation or body concerns. At the betweenpersons level, mean levels of each item interacted with mean self-compassion to predict intuitive eating and body appreciation, but not body concerns or negative affect, consistent with findings that used the composite measure.

Summary of results. Atthe within-persons level, a higher daily frequency of interactions with body-focused others was related to less intuitive eating, lower body appreciation, more body image concerns, and more negative affect on days when self-compassion was lower than usual. On days when self-compassion was higher than usual, its relationship with negative affect disappeared and its association with the three other criteria variables became inversed. At the between-persons level, a higher mean frequency of interactions with body-focused others over the week was negatively related to intuitive eating and body appreciation among individuals with low and average mean levels of self-compassion, but was unrelated to these variables among those with high mean levels of self-compassion.

The present study tested the hypothesis that among college women, displaying a higher level of self-compassion – not just relative to other women (i.e., between-persons) but also relative to personal mean levels (i.e., within-persons) – would be protective in the face of interactions with body-focused others. Findings supported this hypothesis. On days when college women were less self-compassionate than usual, more frequent daily interactions with body-focused others was associated with less intuitive eating and body appreciation, and more body image concerns and negative affect. However, these relationships were either absent or inversed on days when women were more self-compassionate than usual.Asimilar pattern emerged atthe between-persons level.

Among women who had more interactions with body-focused others over the week,those with lower mean levels of self-compassion had less intuitive eating and poorer body appreciation whereas mean frequency of interactions with body-focused others was unrelated to these variables among women with higher levels of self-compassion. Together, results suggest that a higher general level of self-compassion may protect against a higher overall frequency of interactions with body-focused others, and a higher than usual level of self-compassion on a given day may protect against a higher than usual amount of these interactions.

As previously reported by Kelly and Stephen (2016), ICCs revealed that although the young adult women in our study differed from one another in their typical level of self-compassion over the week, a given participant's level of self-compassion still fluctuated a considerable amount from one day to the next, supporting the utility of our current investigation. ICCs also revealed that between-persons differences accounted for 50% ofthe variance in participants'frequency ofinteractions with body-focused others, indicating that there were meaningful differences between young adult women in how often they interacted with body-focused others over the week. However, the fact that the remaining 50% of the variance occurred within-persons reveals thatfrequency ofinteractions with body-focused others also fluctuated a great deal within a person from one day to the next. This was the first study to our knowledge to examine women's self-reported frequency of interactions with body-focused others on a daily basis, and therefore the first to highlight the relative temporal variability of college women's exposure to this potential body image threat. It is also worth noting that based on the mean frequency rating of 2 out of 5, the average college woman's typical day consisted of "some" interactions with body-focused others, a finding which should be replicated in future studies.

Although previous research has found that a higher daily level of self-compassion is associated with better daily body image and eating habits (Breines et al., 2014; Kelly & Stephen, 2016), the present findings are the first to suggest that this within-person variability in self-compassion may have especially important implications for how young adult women feel and behave when faced with threats to their body image. Specifically, we found that a higher-than-usual daily level of self-compassion buffered the positive relationship between daily interactions with body-focused others and indicators of maladaptive functioning (i.e., body image concerns and negative affect) as well as the negative relationships between exposure and indicators of adaptive functioning (i.e., body appreciation and intuitive eating). Especially interesting is that on days when women treated themselves more self-compassionately than usual, a higher frequency of interactions with body-focused others was related to a higher than usual amount of intuitive eating and body appreciation, and a lower than usual amount of negative affect. These findings suggest that a high daily level of self-compassion may not simply protect women fromresponding negatively on days where body-focused social interactions are high, but may actually lead them to display a greater-than-usual tendency to respect their bodies, eat flexibly, and feel better on those days.

Itis interesting to speculate about why this might be. One explanation derives from the fact that there was no within-persons binary relationship between daily interactions with body-focused others and body appreciation, intuitive eating, or negative affect (see Tables 1 and 2). With this in mind, it makes sense that treating oneself with a higher-than-usual amount of self-compassion on these high-interaction days should facilitate more positive functioning than usual, rather than simply maintaining current levels of functioning, which would be evidenced by a nonsignificant relationship between body-focused interactions and criteria variables. Indeed, body image concerns was the only variable that correlated (positively, at a trend-level) with frequency of these interactions,

and thus it makes sense that the relationship between this criterion variable and body-focused interactions was nonsignificant at higher-than-usual levels of daily self-compassion. Taken together, the pattern of results that emerged suggests that at a daily level, more frequent interactions with body-focused others are not problematic for body appreciation, intuitive eating, and affect in and of themselves; however, these interactions may become problematic when individuals are less self-compassionate than usual and may actually be constructive on days when young women are more self-compassionate than usual.

The fact that body-focused social interactions were linked to better body image, eating, and affect on high self-compassion days may also be due to the fact that self-compassion is, at its essence, a response to distress. Although we did not assess the consequences of body-focused interactions during or immediately after their occurrence, past research suggests that these interactions increase momentary levels of distress and body dissatisfaction (Clarke et al., 2010; Stice et al., 2003). More of these interactions on a given day may therefore present women with more episodes of distress and thus more opportunities to respond to their feelings of insecurity. Choosing to respond in a less self-compassionate or more self-critical manner than usual would understandably compromise affect, body appreciation, and intuitive eating on these days. However, responding withmore self-compassionthanusual shouldhelp individuals to routinely adopt a caring orientation toward themselves and their bodies, and as a result experience less negative affect and more intuitive eating and body appreciation on these days. In other words, the presence of multiple body-focused interactionsmight render the benefits of self-compassionate responding more recurrent and pronounced over the day. It would be beneficial for future research to test these ideas and to administer multiple daily assessments to more precisely examine the temporal dynamics of these relationships.

Another finding that emerged in the present analyses was that self-compassion buffered the relationship between frequency of interactions withbody-focusedothers andbothintuitive eating and body appreciation at the between-persons level. Specifically, the young adult women in our sample who had more interactions with body-focused others over the week and who tended to treat themselves withlower or average amounts of self-compassioncompared to their peers ate in a less intuitive manner and appreciated their bodies less. However, mean frequency of interactions with bodyfocused others was unrelated to eating and body image among women who had higher levels of self-compassion over the week. These results are consistent with previous cross-sectional research showing that women who are more self-compassionate may be less negatively affected by more pervasive triggers and correlates of body dissatisfaction (Homan & Tylka, 2015; Kelly, Vimalakanthan, & Carter, 2014; Kelly, Vimalakanthan, & Miller, 2014; Tylka et al., 2015). However, ours are the first findings to show this buffering influence of self-compassion on body image threats atthe betweenpersons level using multiple assessment points.

Post-hoc analyses revealed that all three items that comprised our measure of frequency of interactions with body-focused others tended to interact in a similar manner with self-compassion at the within- and between-persons level. There were only three exceptions, all at the within-persons level. First, self-compassion did not interact with the item assessing interactions with body image focused others to predict negative affect, suggesting that a high daily level of self-compassion was associated with lower distress in the face of interactions with diet- and exercise-focused individuals in particular. In addition, there was no interaction between daily self-compassion and daily interactions with exercise-focused others in predicting body appreciation or body concerns. These findings suggestthat a high daily level of self-compassion may contribute to positive body image and eating on days when young adult

women have more interactions with diet- and body-focused others, but may be less related to body image and eating on days when interactions with exercise-focused others are high. These findings should be replicated, but may suggest that self-compassion is less "necessary" when an individual is exposed to exercise talk, which would be consistent with prior research showing that engaging in exercise talk is not as harmfulto body image as engaging in diettalk and may even be beneficial (Frisén & Holmqvist, 2010; Wasylkiw & Butler, 2013).

Although there has been significant interest in examining the protective role that self-compassion can play when women face threats to their body image, to date, this research has occurred exclusively at the between-persons level. The present study advances this research in important theoretical and practical ways. First, our findings reveal that young adult women's way of coping with body image threats does not just depend on how self-compassionate they are in general. There are actually benefits to being more self-compassionate than usual at times when these potential threats are more frequent, no matter one's typical level of self-compassion. This is a hopeful message as it suggests that if a given woman manages to be more self-compassionate on a given day than usual, she will see benefits in her affect, body image, and eating. These implications stand in contrast to those from between-persons research, which are that young adult women who experience body image stressors will fare better if they are typically more self-compassionate than their peers. Given that this feat will only be possible for certain women, whereas on a given day, all women can be more or less self-compassionate than their customary level, our findings offer far-reaching implications likely to be useful across young adult women. Our results also support the importance of conceptualizing and studying self-compassion not only as an individual difference variable, but also as a state that varies within individuals.

There were several limitations to the present study. First, although we obtained multiple assessment points from each participant, the nature of our analyses made conclusions about the temporal relationships between variables impossible. That is, we cannot conclude, for example,thatthe presence of self-compassion on days with frequent interactions with body-focused others leads to better body image. Second, this was a correlational study and therefore no conclusions about causality can be made. In future research, it would be interesting to manipulate self-compassion while women are faced with varying levels of body image threats to determine whether a similar pattern of results unfolds. It would also be interesting to examine the predictors of day-to-day fluctuations in self-compassion levels.

A third limitation of this study pertains to measurement. First, we relied exclusively on self-report questionnaires. Second, in the interest of keeping daily questionnaires brief to enhance compliance, body image concerns and frequency of interactions with body-focused others were each assessed with only three items. Both measures were face valid, and showed high internal consistency, and the measure of body image concerns displayed evidence of convergent validity; however, results should be replicated with longer, well-validated measures.

It is also important to point out that two of the items from the measure assessing interactions with body-focused others asked about whether others were "focused on" exercise or body image, whereas the other item asked whether others were "talking about" dieting. Although we intended for this measure to assess observ-

able behaviors displayed by interaction partners, it is possible that that measure was also assessing participants' perceptions of their interaction partners' overall exercise and body image concerns. In future research, it would be useful to better disentangle subjective perceptions about others from other people's actual behaviors, and to determine whether self-compassion plays an equally protective role in the face of each.

A fourth limitation of the present study is that we examined relationships between variables at a daily level, but interactions with body-focused others likely fluctuate across even shorter time intervals. For example, one might imagine having lunch with colleagues who are highly body-focused, and then having dinner with friends later in the day who show little body focus. Similarly, self-compassion levels may fluctuate within a day, and not just from one day to the next. In future research, it would be interesting to revisit our research questions while assessing participants at more regular intervals throughout a day. Such an approach would also help to disentangle the temporal relationship between variables. For example, if someone is treating themselves highly self-compassionately on a given morning and then interacts with body-focused others later in the day, does her subsequent body image remain unaffected?

The present findings add to the growing body of literature suggesting that self-compassion may help to protect young adult women from potential body image threats. However, unlike past research, the current results show that young adult women may not need to be more self-compassionate than other women in order to be protected from exposure to recurrent body image threats. Also important is the amount of self-compassion they show themselves relative to their usual level on days when body image threats are higher than usual. Results suggest that teaching young adult women to respond to daily body image stressors by cultivating a higher-than-usual amount of self-compassion may enable them to function and feel better than they ordinarily would on those potentially stressful days.
